name: Liam Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I cover courts and public safety for the Riverside Courier, which is the daily paper and website for our city and the towns around it. Most mornings I'm at the courthouse on Mill Street by nine, sitting in on hearings, then I file a quick web version from the hallway and a longer piece by late afternoon. I like the courtroom, honestly, the way a whole family's week can turn on one sentence from a judge.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The night calls. If there's a bad crash or a stabbing, the desk rings me, and I'm out at a cordon at eleven with my phone, trying to get a word from a police spokesperson. The other thing is the web traffic board on the newsroom wall. Every story has a number next to it, and you can feel the editors watching it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI at the moment, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll use a transcription app on long hearings because typing two hours of evidence by hand is miserable. I tried having a chatbot draft a crime brief once and it got the charge wrong, so I mostly don't trust it for writing. I'm not against it, I just wait until I've seen it work for someone else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what most people in the newsroom would say: told you so. AI got us faster transcripts and maybe a tidier spellcheck, and that's about it. Nobody's replacing the person who sits through a three-day assault trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully calm, because local news was shrinking long before AI came along. The Courier cut six jobs two years ago, and that had nothing to do with chatbots. So a world where AI is hype still leaves me in an industry that loses money on most stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the courts beat and keep the transcription app, because it really does save me about an hour a day. I'd keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings like I do now. Maybe I'd pitch the editor on a monthly long-read about one case from start to finish, because that's the kind of work that builds my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, maybe, because the worry would just go back to being the usual worry about ad money and subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the usual worry. What does that look like on a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth is the managing editor. When my boss closes her office door on a Thursday, everyone in the newsroom goes quiet and checks their phones. Last time it was the photo desk going from three people to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the Courier cut again, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty of options here, which helps. The TV station, the public radio newsroom, a couple of news sites, and the council's press office is always hiring. I'd rather stay a reporter, but I wouldn't starve.

say: I'd tell colleagues AI turned out to be **faster transcripts** and not much else.
I'd say nobody replaces the reporter who **sits through a trial** for three days.
think: I think local news was **already shrinking** before AI, so a plateau doesn't fix that.
I'd be **relieved** about AI but still watching the Courier's money every Thursday.
do: Keep using the **transcription app**, which saves me about an hour a day.
Keep saving **a fifth** each month, as I already do.
Pitch a **monthly long-read** following one court case from start to finish.
feel: I'd feel **mostly fine**, with the old worry about ad money and cuts still there.
S0.quote: When my boss closes her office door on a Thursday, everyone in the newsroom goes quiet and checks their phones.
fieldNote: Liam separates **AI worry** from the older worry about the paper's finances, and the second one is real to him.
His **strong savings** and the many local newsrooms make a job loss survivable, not frightening.
He waits for **proof** before adopting tools, and one bad chatbot draft set him back.

steps.text: Keep covering the courthouse and using the transcription app daily
Keep putting a fifth of each paycheck into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to be smart about it: let the software do the boring bits and keep people where they matter. That's what I'd post too, something sensible, nothing dramatic. I'd probably say the court reporting can't be done from a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the Courier would use this as a reason to stop replacing people. Writing up police press releases and overnight briefs is about a third of my week, and software could do that tomorrow. My own court work is safer, but the newsroom around me gets thinner, and the paper might decide one courts reporter can cover two counties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a colleague who already uses the AI tools, probably Dev on the business desk, to show me his setup properly, and I'd copy it. I'd push harder on the parts that need a body in the room: trials, inquests, sitting with victims' families. And I'd quietly update my CV and have coffee with the editor at the public radio newsroom, just so they know my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then a bit anxious when I think about the briefs going. It's not panic, because I've got savings and options, but I'd feel the floor tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the paper might ask one person to cover two counties. Would you take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for a year. More driving, more hearings, the same pay. I'd do it and keep looking. Saying no to covering two counties for the same pay is how you end up on the next list of job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night editor, Marcus (a colleague in his fifties). His whole shift is tidying copy and writing headlines, which is exactly the stuff the software does. He's got a mortgage and two kids at college, and he's not someone who'd learn new tools quickly.

say: I'd say the paper should let software do **the boring bits** and keep reporters where they matter.
I'd argue that **court reporting** still needs a person sitting in the room.
think: I think the Courier would **stop replacing** people as they leave.
About **a third** is press releases and briefs that software could write tomorrow.
The paper might ask **one courts reporter** to cover two counties.
do: Ask **Dev** to show me his AI setup, then copy it.
Focus my beat on **trials and inquests** where a body in the room matters.
Update my CV and have coffee with the **public radio editor**.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy**, sliding into **anxious** when I picture the briefs going.
S1.quote: Saying no to covering two counties for the same pay is how you end up on the next list of job cuts.
fieldNote: Liam sees the cut coming through **attrition**, not a dramatic layoff, which is realistic for a regional paper.
He would accept **more work** to stay off the list, while quietly looking elsewhere.
His worry for an older colleague was **sharper** than his worry for himself.

steps.text: Sit with Dev on the business desk and copy his AI setup
Meet the public radio newsroom editor for coffee and send an updated CV

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone would say, that it's moving too fast and someone should slow it down. I'd probably post something about how communities still need reporters they can trust. I'd mean it, but I'd know it wouldn't change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job as it exists is gone within two years. If AI can read the court list, pull the charging documents and write a clean story by noon, the Courier won't pay me to do it slower. The only bit left is sitting in the courtroom, and robots don't even matter for that, because a camera feed and a transcript do the job. I'd have maybe a year before the newsroom shrinks to a handful of editors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop spending on anything big; my girlfriend Noor and I were going to look at buying a flat next year, and I'd shelve that. I'd look hard at jobs that need a person physically present, like court clerk or victim support work, and see what training they need. I'd keep working at the Courier as long as they'd pay me, because quitting early would be stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty alarmed, to be honest. Two years isn't long enough to build a whole new career, and at 27 I'd thought the next ten years were going to be about getting better at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned robots don't matter for your job. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because almost nothing I do is hands-on. Typing, phoning, reading, listening, that's all thinking work. The three extra years for robots help a plumber, not me, and the only safe part of my day is being trusted by people in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we should keep renting and stop looking at flats for now. She's a physiotherapist, so her job has the robot delay on its side, and I'd probably say it out loud: my girlfriend Noor is a physiotherapist, so she's probably the safer earner of the two of us now. That would be a strange thing to admit out loud.

say: I'd say it's moving **too fast** and someone should slow it down.
I'd post that towns still need **reporters they can trust**, knowing it changes nothing.
think: I think my **job as it exists** is gone within two years.
Almost all my work is **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help me at all.
The newsroom could shrink to **a handful of editors** within a year.
do: Shelve the **flat purchase** Noor and I planned for next year.
Research **court clerk** and victim support roles and what training they need.
Keep drawing a **Courier paycheck** for as long as they'll pay me.
feel: I'd feel **alarmed**, because two years isn't enough to build a whole new career.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Noor is a physiotherapist, so she's probably the safer earner of the two of us now.
fieldNote: Liam sees his work as **almost entirely thinking work**, so he gets none of the three-year robot delay.
He looks for jobs where **being present** in a room still counts, like court clerk or victim support.
Admitting his partner is now **the safer earner** clearly unsettled him.

steps.text: Stop the flat search with Noor and keep renting
Look up training needed to become a court clerk or victim support worker
Put off any big purchases for at least a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get this right, and newsrooms should use them instead of pretending. I'd probably push the union branch at the Courier to talk about it early. In public I'd sound measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to change direction, but only if I start early. The reporting will get eaten by 2031, I'm sure of that. But five years is long enough to get a qualification and build a reputation somewhere else, which two years never is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in the first year, probably a paralegal certificate, because I already know the courts and the language. I'd keep working full time at the Courier and pay for the course out of savings, maybe four thousand all in. I'd also start using the AI tools properly at work, because knowing them will matter wherever I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the difference between being pushed and stepping off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't paralegal work face AGI too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, fair point, it would. I suppose I picked it because it's close to what I know, not because it's safe. If I'm honest, the part that would last is working with people face to face, and I'd need to think about that more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would your savings go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course, then a bigger rainy-day fund, maybe twelve months instead of eight. I'd still go on holiday with Noor, but somewhere by train rather than a flight.

say: I'd say newsrooms have **a few years** and should use them instead of pretending.
I'd push the Courier's **union branch** to start talking about it early.
think: I think the **reporting** gets eaten by 2031, I'm sure of that.
Five years is long enough to earn **a qualification** and build a reputation elsewhere.
do: Start a part-time **paralegal certificate** in the first year, paid from savings.
Grow the **rainy-day fund** from eight months to twelve.
Learn the **AI tools** properly at work, since they'll matter anywhere.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, more stepping off than being pushed.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get a qualification and build a reputation somewhere else, which two years never is.
fieldNote: The extra time turned Liam from **reacting to planning**, but his worry didn't go away.
When challenged, he admitted his **paralegal choice** was about familiarity rather than safety.
He sees **face-to-face work** as the lasting part, but hasn't worked out what that means yet.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time paralegal certificate costing about four thousand
Build savings from eight months of costs to twelve
Use the newsroom's AI tools on every brief to learn them properly
Raise AI plans at the Courier's union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and our industry shouldn't waste it the way it wasted the internet. That's the line I'd use at the pub with other reporters. Most of them would agree and then do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years takes me to 37, which is still young. I don't have kids, I've got savings, and the city has jobs. So I think I'd be fine, as long as I don't sit there until year nine thinking it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep reporting and get really good at the AI tools, because I'd still be paid to report. Around year three or four I'd decide on a second career, probably something with people in the room, maybe mediation or teaching. I'd keep saving steadily and maybe put some savings into a broad index fund, since the companies building this stuff will do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. Ten years feels like a long runway, even if I know the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most reporters would do nothing. Why would you be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure I would, honestly. I'm the kind of person who waits for proof, and that's dangerous when the proof arrives on the last day. I'd probably need to put a date in my calendar to make myself decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My thirtieth birthday. If I haven't picked a second path by then, I'd have to admit I'm just waiting it out.

say: I'd say our industry **shouldn't waste** ten years the way it wasted the internet.
I'd tell other reporters that **ten years** is a real chance to prepare.
think: I think I'd be **fine at 37**, with no kids, savings and a city full of jobs.
The danger is sitting there **until year nine** thinking it won't happen.
do: Keep reporting and get **really good** at the AI tools for the first few years.
Choose a **second career** with people in the room, like mediation or teaching.
Put part of my savings into a **broad index fund**.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** rather than scared, because ten years is **a long runway**.
S4.quote: I'm the kind of person who waits for proof, and that's dangerous when the proof arrives on the last day.
fieldNote: Liam knows his own **habit of waiting** is the biggest risk in the slow scenario.
He set a **personal deadline**, his thirtieth birthday, to force a decision.
With ten years, his **age and savings** make him feel more secure than in any AGI picture.

steps.text: Pick a second career such as mediation by my thirtieth birthday
Use AI tools daily on the courts beat for the next few years
Move part of my savings into a broad index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Not because I'd starve, but because two years is too short to build anything new, and the Courier would fold before I'd figured out what to do. What would help is proper notice from the paper and some kind of paid retraining, maybe through the union, so people like me aren't paying for courses in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people in court would lose. Families in court trust a local reporter to get their name right, and I'm not sure software writing from a transcript would care about that. I don't think anyone's asked those families.

headlineQuote: Families in court trust a local reporter to get their name right, and I'm not sure software writing from a transcript would care about that.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old courts reporter** at a regional daily, with solid savings and a girlfriend who's a physiotherapist.
He's **pragmatic and steady**, using AI only once he's seen it work for colleagues.
In the mild pictures he worries more about **newspaper finances** than about AI itself.
With **AGI by 2028** he expects his job gone and shelves plans to buy a flat.
With more warning he plans a **second career** and sets his thirtieth birthday as a deadline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to build a new career before the paper folds.
whatWouldHelp: **Proper notice** from the paper and **paid retraining**, perhaps arranged through the union.
